# SIRUP - full documentation

<!-- source: docs/index.md -->

# SIRUP: Spatial Immune Receptor Utilities Package

<div markdown="1" style="background: #ffedcc; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">Under construction</p>
  This site is still under construction. Be aware that some information may be missing or incorrect.
</div>

<img src="img/sirup-logo.png" alt="SIRUP logo" align="right" width="130" style="margin: 0 0 12px 24px;">
SIRUP, the Spatial Immune Receptor Utilities Package, is an R package for working with
spatial adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing (spAIRR-seq) data. 
It works with B cell receptor (BCR) and T cell receptor
(TCR) sequences that have a spatial barcode, together with spatial gene
expression from the same tissue section. Isn't that sweet?

SIRUP helps you:

1. **Process.** Convert demultiplexed long-read spatial immune receptor sequences 
   into high-quality consensus receptor sequences for each spatial location.
   Outputs an [AIRR rearrangement style table](https://docs.airr-community.org/en/latest/datarep/rearrangements.html).
2. **Integrate.** Combine spatially-resolved immune receptors and a Seurat spatial
   transcriptomics object into one unified SIRUP object. The SIRUP object can hold
   multiple spatial tissue sections, as well as associated non-spatial AIRR-seq data
   from bulk or single-cell experiments.
3. **Analyze and visualize.** Select regions of interest through *in silico* micro-dissection,
   measure clonal dominance and diversity within ROIs, test spatial patterns,
   build lineage trees and visualize them over tissue, and more!

<div markdown="1" style="background: #ffedcc; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">Did you know?</p>
  Maple syrup has been spelled [maple sirup](https://maplesyruphistory.com/2022/09/04/the-origins-of-the-spelling-of-maple-sirup-with-an-i/) at different points of U.S. history.
</div>

## Getting started

Start with [Get started with SIRUP](vignettes/get-started.md). It takes about 15
minutes and uses example data that comes with the package. You build a SIRUP
object, plot receptors on the tissue, and measure clonal dominance in a region.

Install SIRUP from GitHub with BiocManager, which will also install dependencies:

```r
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("hoehnlab/SIRUP")
```

Use R 4.1 or later.

## Contents

**Tutorials**

* [Process demultiplexed reads](vignettes/processing.md). Turn
  demultiplexed reads into a table of consensus BCR or TCR sequences.
* [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and

  germinal centers.

  tissue](vignettes/clones-and-trees.md). Build trees with Dowser and show them
  on the H&E image.

  clones](vignettes/spatial-statistics.md). Run Moran's I, Lee's L, Ripley's
  cross K, and join counts.

  blood](vignettes/multisample.md). Combine sections, bulk data, and blood in
  one object.

  object, and the rules that SIRUP checks.

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/choose-spatial-statistic.md -->

Choose a spatial statistic
================

> **Time:** about 8 minutes. **Data:** a small synthetic SIRUP object
> bundled with SIRUP. **Needs:** SIRUP with spdep.

This page helps you pick a spatial statistic. Start from the question
you ask, not from the function name. Each section below names one
question. It then gives the function, the input, and the way to read the
result. A *spot* is one capture location of the spatial assay. A *clone*
is a group of receptors that descend from one ancestor cell.

All tests need a SIRUP object, or a Seurat object with spatial images.
The tests read the spot coordinates from the object. Most tests compare
each spot with its neighbors. You set the neighbors with `k` (the number
of nearest spots) or `radius`.
[Test spatial patterns of genes, cells, and clones](spatial-statistics.md) runs every test on
real data.

## Match the question to the function

| Question | Function | Input |
|----|----|----|
| Is this gene or cell type clustered? | `spatialMoran()` | One gene or numeric metadata column |
| Where are the clusters? | `spatialLocalMoran()` | The same input |
| Do two genes or cell types co-vary? | `spatialLee()` | Two continuous variables |
| Do spots of type A sit near spots of type B? | `spatialRipleyCrossK()` | One metadata column with two labels |
| Does one clone stay together? | `spatialCloneJoinCount()` | Receptor table with clone IDs |
| How far does a clone spread? | `spatialCloneSpread()` | Receptor table with clone IDs |
| How does the repertoire differ between regions? | Polygon summaries | Stored polygons |

## Ask whether a variable clusters

Use `spatialMoran()` to ask if neighboring spots have similar values.
The function computes Moran’s I. This statistic is near 0 when the
values show no spatial pattern. It is positive when similar values sit
together. It is negative when values alternate.

The input is one variable. `variable_type` says what it is: a gene
(`"feature"`), a numeric metadata column (`"metadata"`), receptor
presence (`"receptor"`), or one clone (`"clone"`). For a text metadata
column, give `value` to test one level.

Read $I$ as the size of the pattern. Read the p value as the evidence
for it. A large section gives a tiny p value for a weak pattern.

`spatialLocalMoran()` answers the next question: where are the clusters?
It gives one value for each spot, with a z-score and a p value. Each
spot has its own p value, so adjust for multiple testing.
`plotSpatialLocalMoran()` draws the result on the tissue.

This chunk tests one gene on the synthetic object:

``` r
library(SIRUP)
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
moran <- spatialMoran(x, variable = "gene1", k = 4)
moran$test$estimate[[1]]
#> [1] 0.2176226
moran$test$p.value
#> [1] 0.01873459
```

## Ask whether two variables co-vary

Use `spatialLee()` to ask if two continuous variables share a spatial
pattern. Lee’s L combines Pearson correlation with spatial smoothing. L
is high when both variables are high in the same neighborhoods. The
variables do not need to peak in the same spots.

The input is two continuous variables. Each can be a gene or a numeric
metadata column. Give `x_type`, `y_type`, `assay`, and `layer` as
needed. The result holds `L` and a test. The default test is analytical.
It builds a dense matrix with one entry for each pair of spots. For
large data, such as Visium HD, set `method = "mc"` to use permutations.

Run a positive control. Pick two genes that you expect to share a
pattern. If the control fails, the data or the neighbor setting may be
wrong.

## Ask whether two spot types sit near each other

Use `spatialRipleyCrossK()` to ask if spots of type A lie near spots of
type B. The function counts the type B spots within each distance of an
average type A spot. It compares the curve with curves from random
relabeling.

The input is one metadata column that holds the labels. Give the two
levels as `i` and `j`. Set `nsim` above 0 to get the envelope. Spots
with `NA` in the column are left out.

Read the curve against the envelope. A curve above the envelope means A
and B sit closer than chance. A curve below the envelope means each type
groups with itself. Use `plotRipleyCrossK()` to draw it.

The distance is in image pixels at the stored `image_scale`. Convert it
before you quote a distance in micrometers.

## Ask whether a clone stays together

Use `spatialCloneJoinCount()` to ask if the spots of one clone sit next
to each other. The function marks the spots that hold the clone. It
counts neighbor pairs in which both spots hold the clone. It then calls
`spdep::joincount.test()`.

The input is a receptor table with clone IDs and spatial IDs. A SIRUP
object holds both. By default, the function tests every clone that
occurs in at least `min_spatial_ids` spots. Give `clone_val` to test
chosen clones. If the object has stored polygons, the function runs one
test for each polygon. Set `use_stored_polygons = FALSE` for one test
over the section.

The summary table has one row for each clone. A high `statistic` (a
z-score) and a small `p_value` mean that the clone stays together. The
default alternative is `"greater"`, so the test looks for more joins
than chance.

Moran’s I also accepts one clone with `variable_type = "clone"`. It
treats the clone as a 0/1 value for each spot. The join-count test is
the first choice for clones.

## Ask how far a clone spreads

Use `spatialCloneSpread()` to measure the reach of a clone. It is a
description, not a test. The function reports the mean and the maximum
distance between the points of each clone, for each sample.

``` r
spatialCloneSpread(x)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   sample  clone_id n_spatial_ids mean_pairwise_distance max_pairwise_distance
#>   <chr>   <chr>            <int>                  <dbl>                 <dbl>
#> 1 spatial 1                    5                   2.09                  3.16
#> 2 spatial 2                    7                   2.81                  5   
#> 3 spatial 3                    7                   2.47                  5   
#> 4 spatial 4                   10                   2.44                  5   
#> 5 spatial 5                    7                   2.44                  4.47
```

The input is a receptor table with clone IDs and spatial IDs. A clone
needs at least `min_spatial_ids` points (default 2). By default, each
sequence is a point, so sequences in the same spot give distances of 0.
Set `collapse_within_spot = TRUE` to count each spot once. Distances are
in image pixels.

## Compare regions with polygon summaries

The questions above treat the section as one field. To compare regions
that you drew, use the polygon functions. `polygonReceptorSummary()`
counts receptors, spots, and clones in each polygon.
`spatialCloneDominance()` gives the fraction of receptors in each clone
of each polygon. `polygonDiversity()` gives Hill diversity curves,
rarefied to one size. These functions describe each region. They do not
test a spatial pattern. `polygonDiversity()` leaves out polygons with
fewer than `min_n` receptors.

For the full workflow, see [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md).

## Next steps

- Run every test on real data:
  [Test spatial patterns of genes, cells, and clones](spatial-statistics.md).
- Draw regions and measure their repertoires:
  [Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md).
- Call clones before you test them:
  [Call clones and build lineage trees on the tissue](clones-and-trees.md).

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/clones-and-trees.md -->

Call clones and build lineage trees on the tissue
================

> **Time:** about 20 minutes. **Data:** MG thymus section 2, bundled
> with SIRUP. **Needs:** SIRUP, scoper, dowser, shazam, and the IMGT
> reference sequences for the germline and tree steps.

A clone is a group of B or T cells that descend from one ancestor cell
and share its receptor rearrangement. In this page, you call clones in a
SIRUP object and build a lineage tree for some of them. A lineage tree
shows how the sequences of one clone relate to each other. Each tip of
the tree is one sequence. You then pair each tree with the tissue, so
you can see where each tip sits. At the end, you compare distances in
the tree with distances on the tissue.

SIRUP does not reimplement clone calling or tree building. It runs the
Immcantation tools (scoper, dowser, shazam) on the receptor table inside
the SIRUP object. It then adds the spatial part: clone maps, trees
paired with tissue plots, and distances between tips in and between
regions.

## Load the data

This page uses MG thymus section 2 and its polygons. Each polygon
outlines one ectopic germinal center (eGC). An eGC is a site in the
thymus where B cells proliferate and mutate their receptors. The data
are bundled with SIRUP.

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

``` r
extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "SIRUP")

thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
bcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz")) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  ) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = gsub(",", "_", sequence_id)) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL,
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))
#> filterAirr kept 2189 of 3793 rows (dropped 1604).

sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = bcrs,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)
```

The code replaces the comma in each `sequence_id` with `_`. dowser
writes trees in Newick format, and a comma separates tips in that
format. dowser therefore renames tips that contain a comma. With the
comma gone, the tip names match the receptor table. SIRUP can then find
each tip on the tissue.

## Call clones

The object has no clones yet. To call clones, run
`scoper::hierarchicalClones()` through `updateReceptors()`.
`updateReceptors()` gives the receptor table to the function as its
first argument, with your other arguments. It then stores the returned
table and validates the object.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
#> Warning: package 'scoper' was built under R version 4.5.3

sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 2,105 receptor sequences x 67 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
#> Polygons:        9
dplyr::n_distinct(getReceptors(sirup)$clone_id)
#> [1] 953
```

`hierarchicalClones()` groups sequences with the same V gene, J gene,
and junction length. It joins sequences whose junctions differ by less
than `threshold`. The SIRUP paper used `threshold = 0.1` for BCRs. TCRs
do not mutate, so call TCR clones with `scoper::identicalClones()`.

The function writes a `clone_id` column. `updateReceptors()` records it
as the clone field. If a function writes a different column, record it
with `receptor_fields = list(clone = "my_clone_column")`.

## Reconstruct germlines

The germline of a clone is the sequence of its unmutated ancestor. A
lineage tree starts at this sequence. `dowser::createGermlines()`
reconstructs one germline for each clone from the IMGT reference
sequences. IMGT is the international database of immune receptor genes.
The SIRUP paper made the germlines in the object and removed likely PCR
chimeras.

SIRUP does not include the IMGT references. Download them, for example
with the Immcantation script `fetch_imgtdb.sh`. Then set the environment
variable `SIRUP_IMGT_DIR` to the folder that holds the human V, D, and J
FASTA files, such as `~/share/germlines/imgt/human/vdj`. The germline
and tree chunks on this page run only when that folder exists.

``` r
references <- dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir)
#> [1] "Read in 1198 from 17 fasta files"

sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  references = references,
  id = "sequence_id",
  nproc = 1
)

sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, function(receptors) {
  chimera <- shazam::slideWindowDb(
    receptors,
    sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
    germlineColumn = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
    mutThresh = 6,
    windowSize = 10
  )
  receptors[!chimera, ]
})
```

## Measure somatic hypermutation

Somatic hypermutation (SHM) is the process that introduces point
mutations into B cell receptor genes. `shazam::observedMutations()`
counts the mutations of each sequence against a germline. With clonal
germlines, use `germline_alignment_d_mask`. The chunk below uses
`germline_alignment`, the germline that IgBLAST wrote for each sequence.
This choice lets the chunk run without the IMGT references. The result
goes in `mu_freq`, the fraction of mutated positions.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  shazam::observedMutations,
  sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
  germlineColumn = "germline_alignment",
  frequency = TRUE,
  combine = TRUE
)
summary(getReceptors(sirup)$mu_freq)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#> 0.00000 0.01462 0.03750 0.04184 0.06377 0.13467
```

`plotReceptors()` can color spots by a numeric receptor column. Give the
column to `value`. If a spot has several receptors, `value_combine` sets
how SIRUP combines them. The default is the mean.

``` r
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  group = "locus",
  value = "mu_freq",
  value_colors = c("white", "darkred"),
  receptor_size = 1.3,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  title = "Mean SHM frequency per spot"
)
```

![](clones-and-trees_files/figure-gfm/shm-map-1.jpeg)

## Choose clones

Trees are most useful for expanded clones. The code below keeps clones
that have 10 to 60 sequences and at least one sequence in an eGC. It
sorts them by the number of sequences in eGCs.

``` r
clone_sizes <- getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  group_by(clone_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_sequences = n(),
    n_in_gc = sum(!is.na(polygon_id)),
    n_gcs = n_distinct(na.omit(polygon_id)),
    gcs = paste(sort(unique(na.omit(polygon_id))), collapse = ", ")
  ) %>%
  filter(n_sequences >= 10, n_sequences <= 60, n_in_gc > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_in_gc))

head(clone_sizes)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   clone_id n_sequences n_in_gc n_gcs gcs  
#>   <chr>          <int>   <int> <int> <chr>
#> 1 739               15       6     2 6, 7 
#> 2 810               13       6     1 5    
#> 3 196               40       5     2 3, 5 
#> 4 604               12       3     2 5, 6 
#> 5 428               11       2     1 5    
#> 6 598               13       1     1 7
tree_clones <- head(clone_sizes$clone_id, 3)
```

Plot the spots of the three chosen clones. A spot is one capture area of
the Visium slide.

``` r
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  group = "clone_id",
  group_val = tree_clones,
  receptor_size = 1.6,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  zoom = TRUE,
  title = "Selected clones"
)
```

![](clones-and-trees_files/figure-gfm/clone-map-1.jpeg)

## Build trees

Two functions run dowser on the object. `formatSpatialClones()` runs
`dowser::formatClones()` and stores the result as an analysis.
`getSpatialTrees()` runs `dowser::getTrees()` on a stored
formatted-clone analysis and stores the trees as another analysis. Both
functions take the dowser arguments.

Tree building takes time for large clones. First make a smaller object
with only the clones that you want. `updateReceptors()` with
`dplyr::filter()` does this.

``` r
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id %in% tree_clones)

tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  analysis_name = "formatted_clones",
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "polygon_id")
)

set.seed(1)
tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(
  tree_sirup,
  f_clones_analysis = "formatted_clones",
  analysis_name = "trees",
  build = "pratchet"
)

trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees")
trees
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   clone_id data       locus  seqs trees  
#>   <chr>    <list>     <chr> <int> <list> 
#> 1 196      <airrClon> IGH      38 <phylo>
#> 2 739      <airrClon> IGH      15 <phylo>
#> 3 810      <airrClon> IGH      13 <phylo>
```

`traits` keeps the columns that the tree plots need. Keep the spatial
ID, so SIRUP can put each tip on the tissue. Add any column that you
want to color by.

`build = "pratchet"` builds maximum parsimony trees, which is fast. The
SIRUP paper used maximum likelihood (`build = "pml"`). For B cell
models, use IgPhyML (`build = "igphyml"` with the `igphyml` path).

> **Note.** By default, `formatClones()` merges identical sequences into
> one tip. A tip can then stand for several sequences.

Store the trees in the main object.

``` r
sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "trees", trees)
```

## Pair each tree with the tissue

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` makes two plots for each clone: the
lineage tree and a tissue map. Each tip has one color in both plots. You
can find a tip of the tree on the tissue.

``` r
pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  trees,
  object = sirup,
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black"
)
#> Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
#> ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.
#> ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the ggtree package.
#>   Please report the issue at <https://github.com/YuLab-SMU/ggtree/issues>.
#> This warning is displayed once per session.
#> Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
#> generated.
names(pairs)
#> [1] "196" "739" "810"

cowplot::plot_grid(
  pairs[[1]]$tree,
  pairs[[1]]$spatial_clone,
  rel_widths = c(1.2, 1)
)
```

![](clones-and-trees_files/figure-gfm/tree-pairs-1.jpeg)

The result is a list with one element for each clone. Each element holds
a `tree` plot and a `spatial_clone` plot. Tips with a spot in this
section are circles. Tips without a spot, such as bulk sequences, are
squares and appear in the tree only. Sequences in the same spot share a
point on the map.

### Color tips by group

A clone with many tips is hard to read when each tip has its own color.
`clusterTreesTips()` cuts each tree into `k` connected groups of related
tips. The code below uses `k = 4` for every tree.

``` r
clustered <- clusterTreesTips(
  trees,
  k = 4,
  id = "sequence_id",
  cluster = "tree_cluster"
)

cluster_pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  clustered,
  object = sirup,
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = TRUE
)

cowplot::plot_grid(
  cowplot::plot_grid(
    cluster_pairs[[1]]$tree,
    cluster_pairs[[1]]$spatial_clone,
    rel_widths = c(1.2, 1)
  ),
  cluster_pairs[[1]]$legend,
  ncol = 1,
  rel_heights = c(1, cluster_pairs[[1]]$legend_rel_height)
)
```

![](clones-and-trees_files/figure-gfm/tree-clusters-1.jpeg)

With `k = "auto"`, the function chooses `k` for each tree from
`k_range`. It stops when one more cut reduces the mean within-group
patristic distance by less than `improvement_threshold`. The default is
10%. A tree with little structure can get `k = 1`, which gives all its
tips one color.

`color_by` accepts any column of the dowser clone data. For example,
`color_by = "polygon_id"` colors each tip by its eGC, because the code
kept `polygon_id` in `traits`.

> **Tip.**
> `spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF(cluster_pairs, "tree_pairs.pdf", width = 12, height = 6)`
> writes one page for each clone.

## Compare tree distance with physical distance

Do sequences in the same eGC have shorter tree distances than sequences
in different eGCs? The patristic distance between two tips is the sum of
the branch lengths between them. `tipPatristicMatrix()` gives these
distances for a set of tips.

The code below takes the selected clone that spans the most eGCs. It
compares the tip pairs in the same eGC with the tip pairs in different
eGCs.

``` r
multi_gc_clone <- clone_sizes %>%
  filter(clone_id %in% tree_clones) %>%
  slice_max(n_gcs, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  pull(clone_id)
multi_gc_clone
#> [1] "739"

index <- which(trees$clone_id == multi_gc_clone)
clone_data <- trees$data[[index]]@data
tree <- trees$trees[[index]]

gc_tips <- clone_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(polygon_id), sequence_id %in% tree$tip.label) %>%
  select(sequence_id, polygon_id)

distances <- tipPatristicMatrix(tree, gc_tips$sequence_id)

pairs_table <- as.data.frame(as.table(distances)) %>%
  rename(tip_a = Var1, tip_b = Var2, distance = Freq) %>%
  filter(as.character(tip_a) < as.character(tip_b)) %>%
  mutate(
    gc_a = gc_tips$polygon_id[match(tip_a, gc_tips$sequence_id)],
    gc_b = gc_tips$polygon_id[match(tip_b, gc_tips$sequence_id)],
    pair = if_else(gc_a == gc_b, "same eGC", "different eGCs")
  )

pairs_table %>%
  group_by(pair) %>%
  summarise(n_pairs = n(), median_distance = median(distance))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   pair           n_pairs median_distance
#>   <chr>            <int>           <dbl>
#> 1 different eGCs       5          0.0273
#> 2 same eGC            10          0.0150
```

Read the two medians in the table. One clone cannot support a
conclusion, because tip pairs share branches. The SIRUP paper ran this
comparison over all eGC clones. It used a mixed model with a random
effect for each clone.

- Add more sections, bulk AIRR-seq, and blood tips to a tree:
  [Analyze several sections with bulk AIRR-seq and blood](multisample.md).
- Learn how SIRUP stores trees and other results:

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/get-started.md -->

Get started with SIRUP
================

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<b>Time</b>: ~15 minutes. <b>Data</b>: example MG thymus data in SIRUP.

</div>

Here, we will build a SIRUP object from example data and run a few
simple analyses.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #9e584a; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #8b3620; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

This page starts after read processing. If you have raw or demultiplexed
reads, see [Process demultiplexed reads](processing.md) first.

</div>

## Install SIRUP

Install SIRUP and its dependencies from GitHub with BiocManager:

``` r
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("hoehnlab/SIRUP")
```

This vignette uses a few of SIRUP’s suggested packages as well. Run the
code below to install any that are missing:

``` r
packages <- c("spatstat.explore", "spatstat.geom", "spatstat.random", "pals")
missing <- packages[!vapply(packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing) > 0) install.packages(missing)
```

## Look at the example data

SIRUP includes an example spAIRR-seq data set from the thymus of a
patient with myasthenia gravis (MG). The thymus in MG can contain
ectopic germinal centers (eGCs) where B cells undergo affinity
maturation. The data were generated with 10x Visium for spatial
transcriptomics and barcodes, then RAGE-seq + long-read Oxford Nanopore
sequencing to amplify BCRs/TCRs and sequence them.

This vignette uses these files:

| File | Contents |
|----|----|
| `mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds` | A spatial Seurat object for MG thymus |
| `mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz` | AIRR rearrangement table of IGH sequences with spatial IDs |
| `mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv` | Annotated polygons of the eGCs |
| `mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz` | Cell-type proportions for each spot |

The files are in the `extdata` folder of the package. This code finds
the folder:

``` r
extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "SIRUP")
```

The SIRUP paper describes how the authors made these files. To reduce
file sizes, each Seurat object holds a few hundred genes and a reduced
image.

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Load the spatial GEX data and the receptors

Read the Seurat object and the AIRR table:

``` r
thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
thymus
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 506 features across 3203 samples within 2 assays 
#> Active assay: Spatial (449 features, 0 variable features)
#>  2 layers present: counts, data
#>  1 other assay present: alra
#>  1 spatial field of view present: thymus_slice2

bcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz"))
bcrs %>%
  select(sequence_id, v_call, j_call, c_call, sequence_alignment) %>%
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   sequence_id         v_call                    j_call c_call sequence_alignment
#>   <chr>               <chr>                     <chr>  <chr>  <chr>             
#> 1 9,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV2-5*02                IGHJ4… IGHG1  ...ATCACCTTGAAGGA…
#> 2 11,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT IGHV3-30*03,IGHV3-30*06   IGHJ4… IGHG1  .................…
#> 3 2,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV5-51*01               IGHJ5… IGHG2  GAGGTGCCGCTGGTGCA…
#> 4 6,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV5-51*01               IGHJ5… IGHG2  GAGGTGCCGCTGGTGCA…
#> 5 5,CCTACATTCACAGACG  IGHV3-23*01,IGHV3-23*04,… IGHJ4… IGHG1  .................…
#> 6 3,CCTACATTCACAGACG  IGHV1-2*02,IGHV1-2*04     IGHJ4… IGHG1  CAGGTGCATCTGGTGCA…
```

Each row is one BCR sequence. The processing pipeline wrote the spatial
ID at the end of `sequence_id`, after a comma.

## Match each sequence to a spot

`extractSpatialIds()` is a convenience function to extract the spatial
ID and put it into its own column. The `regex` argument finds the
spatial ID. The `suffix` argument adds `-1`, so that each spatial ID
matches a spot name in the Seurat object.

``` r
bcrs <- extractSpatialIds(
  bcrs,
  id = "sequence_id",
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
  suffix = "-1"
)

head(colnames(thymus))
#> [1] "AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1" "AAACACCAATAACTGC-1" "AAACAGCTTTCAGAAG-1"
#> [4] "AAACAGGGTCTATATT-1" "AAACAGTGTTCCTGGG-1" "AAACATGGTGAGAGGA-1"
mean(bcrs$barcode_10x %in% colnames(thymus))
#> [1] 0.9372528
```

A few sequences have a spatial ID that is not in the Seurat object. The
spot was likely off the tissue or failed the expression quality control.
SIRUP will maintain these receptor sequences in the integrated SIRUP
object, but it will not be able to place them in spatial plots.

## Filter the sequences

Keep only the high-quality sequences. The thresholds used are discussed
in [Process demultiplexed reads](processing.md).

``` r
bcrs <- filterAirr(
  bcrs,
  locus_val = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 250,
  min_j_length = 30,
  min_junction_length = 10,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  min_consensus_count = NULL,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
)
#> filterAirr kept 2189 of 3793 rows (dropped 1604).
```

## Create a SIRUP object

`createSIRUP()` joins the Seurat object and the receptor table. Tell it
which receptor column holds the spatial ID and which holds the locus.
You can also specify the image scale and coordinate settings when
constructing the object, which are discussed further below.

``` r
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = bcrs,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  locus = "locus",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  metadata = list(tissue = "MG thymus", section = "slice 2")
)

sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 2,189 receptor sequences x 56 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 817/888 receptor IDs in spatial data (92.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Analyses:        0

summary(sirup)
#> SIRUP summary
#>   Spatial IDs:      3,203
#>   Receptor records: 2,189
#>   Receptor IDs:     888
#>   Matched IDs:      817 (92.0%)
#>   Matched records:  2,047
#>   Image scale:      lowres
#>   Swap coords:      FALSE
#>   Stored analyses:  0
#> 
#> Per-sample summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   sample  n_spatial_ids n_receptor_records n_receptor_ids n_matched_ids
#>   <chr>           <int>              <int>          <int>         <int>
#> 1 spatial          3203               2189            888           817
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: n_matched_records <int>, id_match_rate <dbl>
```

If a `spatial_id`, `locus`, and/or `clone` column are specified when
constructing the SIRUP object, later functions can find these columns
without including them as arguments.

Two settings control how SIRUP constructs plots over the H&E image:

- `image_scale` is `"lowres"` or `"hires"`. Use the image that tge
  Seurat object stores. `Load10X_Spatial()` stores the low-resolution
  image by default, though it can use the high-resolution image if
  specified in the `image.name` argument.
- `swap_coords` swaps the x and y coordinates. Set it to `TRUE` if the
  spots have the right shape but sit rotated or mirrored over the image.
  This is easiest to determine by plotting the spots as shown below.

``` r
coords <- SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates(thymus)
ggplot(coords, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() 
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/check-swapcoords-1.jpeg)

If both arguments are included when constructing the SIRUP object, they
will be stored in the object, and plotting functions will automatically
use them. If they are not specified when constructing the SIRUP object,
both settings should be passed to any plotting functions.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #9e584a; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #8b3620; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

[How the SIRUP object works](sirup-object.md) discusses the SIRUP object
in more detail.

</div>

## Building clones in the SIRUP object

A clone is a group of cells that descend from a common ancestor. Many
SIRUP functions work with clone-level data, but SIRUP does not itself
build clones. The `updateReceptors()` function is a method that can runs
any function on the receptor table and updates the receptor table in the
object with the result. This call runs `hierarchicalClones()` from the
`scoper` package.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
#> Warning in prepare_db(db = db, junction = junction, v_call = v_call, j_call =
#> j_call, : Removed 84 sequences with non ATCG characters.
#> Running defineClonesScoper in bulk mode and only keep heavy chains
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 2,105 receptor sequences x 57 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
```

The receptor table now has a `clone_id` column, and SIRUP records it as
the clone field in the object automatically.

## Plot gene expression and receptors on the tissue

`spatialExpressionPlot()` plots gene expression over the H&E image. By
default, it hides spots with zero expression to help the tissue stay
visible, though this can be turned off by setting `zero_tol = -Inf`.

The example object has two assays: `Spatial` (counts and log-normalized
data) and `alra` (ALRA-imputed values), which can help improve
visualization. *AICDA* is a marker for germinal center B cells, and it
is plotted below.

``` r
spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  title = "AICDA",
  zero_tol = 0,
  point_alpha = 0.5
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/expression-1.jpeg)

`plotReceptors()` plots all spots that have a receptor. The `group`
argument is the receptor column that determines the color. All BCRs here
are IGH, so they all are colored the same.

``` r
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  group = "locus",
  colors = "#0072B2",
  receptor_size = 1.2,
  title = "BCR-positive spots"
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/receptors-1.jpeg)

To restrict a receptors plot to a set with only a particular value of
the `group` column, use the `group_val` argument. This plot includes
only the three largest IGH clones.

``` r
top_clones <- getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  count(clone_id, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>%
  pull(clone_id)
top_clones
#> [1] "34"  "288" "196"

plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  group = "clone_id",
  group_val = top_clones,
  overlap = "average",
  receptor_size = 1.6,
  title = "Three largest clones"
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/clones-1.jpeg)

Because this data was generated with 10X Visium spatial sequencing, each
spot likely contains multiple cells. Resultingly, sequences from
distinct groups may share a spot. By default, `plotReceptors()` gives
the spot a combined label and averages the colors of the two groups. The
`overlap` argument controls this behavior.

`plotReceptorsExpression()` combines the two plots. Spots with gene
expression are filled points. Spots with a receptor have a hollow ring
on top:

``` r
plotReceptorsExpression(
  sirup,
  group = "locus",
  gene = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  colors = "#0072B2",
  receptor_size = 1.3,
  feature_size = 2,
  title = "AICDA expression and BCR-positive spots"
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/receptors-expression-1.jpeg)

## *In silico* micro-dissection of ROIs

Many spatial questions concern a particular region, such as a germinal
center, a tumor margin, or a lesion. `selectSpatialPolygons()` opens an
app where users can draw polygons over regions of interest using the H&E
image and gene expression (e.g., *AICDA*) or spatial object metadata.

``` r
gc_vertices <- selectSpatialPolygons(
  sirup,
  feature = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  plot_image = TRUE,
  save_path = "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"
)
```

![](figures/polygon-app.jpg)

Click around the edge of a region. Each click snaps to the nearest spot.
**Close polygon** joins the last vertex to the first:

![](figures/polygon-click-1.png)![](figures/polygon-click-2.png)![](figures/polygon-closed.png)

After you click **Done**, the app returns the vertices of every polygon.
It writes them to the CSV file at `save_path` (which can be changed
using the CSV path in the app).

`addPolygons()` attaches polygons to the object. Give it the data frame
from the app (`polygons = gc_vertices`) or the CSV file
(`polygons_path`). SIRUP then determines which polygons, if any, contain
each spot and each receptor. The example data include the annotated eGC
polygons from the SIRUP paper.

``` r
sirup <- addPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)

getPolygons(sirup)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   polygon_id vertices        
#>   <chr>      <named list>    
#> 1 1          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 2 2          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 3 3          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 4 4          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 5 5          <tibble [6 × 5]>
#> 6 6          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 7 7          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 8 8          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 9 9          <tibble [4 × 5]>

getPolygons(sirup)$vertices[[1]]
#> # A tibble: 7 × 5
#>   spatial_id             x     y image         .sirup_polygon_label
#>   <chr>              <dbl> <dbl> <chr>         <chr>               
#> 1 ATCGACCCAATACAGA-1  300.  327. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 2 AGTTCCTATTTATGTT-1  307.  327. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 3 CAGTCTGTATACTGGG-1  310.  320. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 4 GCGCCGTTCCACGATA-1  307.  314. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 5 TTATGAATGAAAGGGA-1  300.  314. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 6 ACATCGATCGTTTACC-1  296.  320. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 7 ATCGACCCAATACAGA-1  300.  327. thymus_slice2 1
```

Plot the polygons over the H&E image with `plotSpatialPolygons()`.

``` r
plotSpatialPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygon_alpha = 0.3,
  label_outside = TRUE,
  label_offset = 0.02,
  label_color = "white",
  label_leader = FALSE
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/plot-spatial-polygons-1.jpeg)

The receptor table now has a `polygon_id` column. Receptors outside
every polygon get `NA`:

``` r
getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  count(polygon_id)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   polygon_id     n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 1             28
#> 2 2             23
#> 3 3             14
#> 4 5             47
#> 5 6              4
#> 6 7             30
#> 7 8              6
#> 8 9              4
#> 9 <NA>        1949
```

## Determine which clones dominate the polygons

`polygonReceptorSummary()` counts the receptors, spots, and clones in
each polygon. It stores the result in the object as an analysis.

``` r
sirup <- polygonReceptorSummary(sirup, polygon_id = "polygon_id")
getAnalysis(sirup, "polygon_receptor_summary")
#> # A tibble: 9 × 5
#>   polygon_id n_receptors n_spatial_ids n_clones top_clone_fraction
#>   <chr>            <int>         <int>    <int>              <dbl>
#> 1 1                   28             6       16              0.143
#> 2 2                   23             3       16              0.174
#> 3 3                   14             3        8              0.286
#> 4 4                    0             0        0             NA    
#> 5 5                   47            12       23              0.128
#> 6 6                    4             4        4              0.25 
#> 7 7                   30             8       12              0.167
#> 8 8                    6             3        4              0.333
#> 9 9                    4             3        4              0.25
```

Clonal dominance measures how much of a region the largest clones fill.
`spatialCloneDominance()` computes the fraction of the receptors in each
polygon that belongs to each clone. `plotSpatialPolygonPies()` draws one
pie chart (or stacked bar chart) for each polygon next to the tissue.

``` r
dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(object = sirup)

dominance$dominance %>%
  group_by(polygon) %>%
  slice_max(proportion, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(polygon, clone_id, n_receptors, proportion)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#> # Groups:   polygon [8]
#>   polygon clone_id n_receptors proportion
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 1       928                4      0.143
#> 2 2       381                4      0.174
#> 3 3       196                4      0.286
#> 4 5       810                6      0.128
#> 5 6       136                1      0.25 
#> 6 7       739                5      0.167
#> 7 8       242                2      0.333
#> 8 9       222                1      0.25

pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  fill = "clone_id",
  top_n = 5
)
pies$page_1
#> Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_text()`).
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/dominance-1.jpeg)

The function returns one plot for each page, with six pies on a page.
The `top_n` argument sets how many clones get their own color in each
pie. The grey `Other` slice holds the remaining clones.

[Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md) covers ROIs in more detail.

## Save an analysis in a SIRUP object

`setAnalysis()` stores analysis within the SIRUP object. Stored analyses
can be accessed with `getAnalysis()`.

``` r
sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "gc_dominance", dominance)
listAnalyses(sirup)
#> [1] "polygon_receptor_summary" "gc_dominance"

getAnalysis(sirup, "gc_dominance") %>% str()
#> List of 6
#>  $ dominance         :'data.frame':  87 obs. of  11 variables:
#>   ..$ clone_id             : chr [1:87] "928" "720" "859" "17" ...
#>   ..$ v_gene               : chr [1:87] "IGHV4-61*01" "IGHV3-7*04" "IGHV4-34*01" "IGHV5-51*01" ...
#>   ..$ v_gene_family        : chr [1:87] "IGHV4-61" "IGHV3-7" "IGHV4-34" "IGHV5-51" ...
#>   ..$ v_gene_superfamily   : chr [1:87] "IGHV4" "IGHV3" "IGHV4" "IGHV5" ...
#>   ..$ n_receptors          : num [1:87] 4 3 3 2 2 2 2 2 1 1 ...
#>   ..$ proportion           : num [1:87] 0.1429 0.1071 0.1071 0.0714 0.0714 ...
#>   ..$ region_receptor_total: num [1:87] 28 28 28 28 28 28 28 28 28 28 ...
#>   ..$ n_region_spatial_ids : int [1:87] 7 7 7 7 7 7 7 7 7 7 ...
#>   ..$ polygon              : chr [1:87] "1" "1" "1" "1" ...

#>   ..$ polygon_label        : chr [1:87] "1" "1" "1" "1" ...

#>   ..$ spatial_id: chr [1:55] "ACATCGATCGTTTACC-1" "AGTTCCTATTTATGTT-1" "ATCGACCCAATACAGA-1" "CAGTCTGTATACTGGG-1" ...
#>   ..$ polygon   : chr [1:55] "1" "1" "1" "1" ...
#>   ..$ polygon_id: chr [1:55] "1" "1" "1" "1" ...
#>  $ region_coordinates:'data.frame':  55 obs. of  9 variables:
#>   ..$ cell             : chr [1:55] "ACATCGATCGTTTACC-1" "AGTTCCTATTTATGTT-1" "ATCGACCCAATACAGA-1" "CAGTCTGTATACTGGG-1" ...
#>   ..$ x                : num [1:55] 296 307 300 310 303 ...
#>   ..$ y                : num [1:55] 320 327 327 320 320 ...
```

## Save and read a SIRUP object

`saveSIRUP()` writes the object to one RDS file. `readSIRUP()` reads it
back and validates it.

``` r
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_thymus_slice2.sirup.rds")
saveSIRUP(sirup, path)
sirup <- readSIRUP(path)
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 2,105 receptor sequences x 67 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        2
#> Polygons:        9
```

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/multisample.md -->

Analyze several sections with bulk AIRR-seq and blood
================

> **Time:** about 25 minutes. **Data:** two MG thymus sections, bulk
> thymus BCR-seq, and bulk blood BCR-seq, bundled with SIRUP. **Needs:**
> SIRUP, scoper, and dowser. The tree step also needs the IMGT reference
> sequences.

Most studies have more than one tissue section. You can also have bulk
AIRR-seq of the same tissue, or blood from other time points. In this
page, you put all of these samples in one SIRUP object. You call clones
on all samples together. You then ask where each clone was seen, compare
clonal dominance in each section, and build a lineage tree that has
blood tips.

A clone is a group of B or T cells that descend from one ancestor cell
and share its receptor rearrangement. If you call clones on all samples
together, one clone ID names the same lineage in every sample.

One SIRUP object can hold all of this:

- `spatial` can be a named list of Seurat objects, one for each section.
- The receptor table holds the rows from every section and every bulk
  sample. A `sample` column tells SIRUP which sample each row belongs
  to.
- Rows whose `sample` does not name a section stay in the table as
  nonspatial rows. SIRUP does not put them on a tissue. Clone calling,
  trees, and your own summaries can use them.

This page follows Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper. The MG thymus data come
from a patient who had a thymectomy. Besides the two Visium sections,
there is bulk BCR-seq of the thymus. There is also bulk BCR-seq of
blood, taken at the thymectomy and 12 months later. The question is
which clones in ectopic germinal centers (eGCs) also appear in the
blood. An eGC is a site in the thymus where B cells proliferate and
mutate their receptors.

## Load the samples

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

``` r
extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "SIRUP")

spatial <- list(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds")),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
)

read_bcrs <- function(file, sample, compartment) {
  airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, file)) %>%
    mutate(sample = sample, compartment = compartment)
}

sections <- bind_rows(
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice1"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2", "thymus_slice2")
) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  )

bulk <- bind_rows(
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_thymus_1", "bulk_thymus"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_thymus_2", "bulk_thymus"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month0_1", "blood_month0"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month0_2", "blood_month0"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month12_1", "blood_month12"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month12_2", "blood_month12")
)

bcrs <- bind_rows(sections, bulk) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))
#> filterAirr kept 5733 of 8849 rows (dropped 3116).

count(bcrs, compartment, sample)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   compartment   sample                   n
#>   <chr>         <chr>                <int>
#> 1 blood_month0  bulk_blood_month0_1    182
#> 2 blood_month0  bulk_blood_month0_2    182
#> 3 blood_month12 bulk_blood_month12_1   241
#> 4 blood_month12 bulk_blood_month12_2   108
#> 5 bulk_thymus   bulk_thymus_1          176
#> 6 bulk_thymus   bulk_thymus_2          576
#> 7 thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1      1967
#> 8 thymus_slice2 mg_thymus_slice2      2105
```

`read_bcrs()` reads one AIRR file and adds two columns: `sample` and
`compartment`. After the barcodes come out of the section IDs, the code
makes each `sequence_id` unique and safe for trees. It puts the sample
name in front, because IDs repeat between files. It replaces the comma
with `_`, because dowser renames tree tips that contain a comma.

The section rows get a `sample` that matches the names of the `spatial`
list. The bulk and blood rows have their own sample names and no
barcode.

> **Note.** To keep the package small, the bulk files hold a subset of
> the bulk data. They hold the blood sequences of clones seen in a
> section. They also hold up to 10 bulk thymus sequences of each clone
> that reaches the blood.

## Create a multi-sample object

Give `createSIRUP()` the named list and the name of the `sample` column.

``` r
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = spatial,
  receptors = bcrs,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  sample = "sample",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)

sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 6,599 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 2 spatial samples, 2 images
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 5,537 receptor sequences x 58 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 1,567/1,640 receptor IDs in spatial data (95.5%)
#> Samples:         2
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Sample ID field: sample
#> Analyses:        0
spatialSamples(sirup)
#> [1] "mg_thymus_slice1" "mg_thymus_slice2"
```

Visium barcodes repeat between sections. For example,
`AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1` exists in both. SIRUP matches each receptor to a
spot by the pair of sample and barcode, so the two sections never mix. A
spot is one capture area of the Visium slide.

If the sections need different image settings, give named values:
`image_scale = c(mg_thymus_slice1 = "hires", mg_thymus_slice2 = "lowres")`.

## Get one sample

The accessors take a `sample` argument.

``` r
getSpatial(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1")
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 506 features across 3396 samples within 2 assays 
#> Active assay: Spatial (449 features, 0 variable features)
#>  2 layers present: counts, data
#>  1 other assay present: alra
#>  1 spatial field of view present: thymus_slice1
nrow(getReceptors(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1"))
#> [1] 1967
nrow(getReceptors(sirup))
#> [1] 5537
```

`filterSample()` returns a new SIRUP object with one section. It drops
the nonspatial rows.

``` r
slice1 <- filterSample(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1")
slice1
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,396 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 1,967 receptor sequences x 58 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 770/772 receptor IDs in spatial data (99.7%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Analyses:        0
```

`subsetSIRUP()` gives finer control. It can keep a set of spots or a set
of receptor rows. With `keep_nonspatial_receptors = TRUE`, it also keeps
the bulk rows.

`mergeSIRUP()` goes the other way. It combines single-section objects
into a multi-sample object, and it adds a sample column with the names
that you give.

``` r
slice2 <- filterSample(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice2")
merged <- mergeSIRUP(
  slice1, slice2,
  samples = c("mg_thymus_slice1", "mg_thymus_slice2"),
  sample_field = "sample"
)
merged
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 6,599 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 2 spatial samples, 2 images
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 4,072 receptor sequences x 58 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 1,567/1,640 receptor IDs in spatial data (95.5%)
#> Samples:         2
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Sample ID field: sample
#> Analyses:        0
```

## Add polygons for each section

A polygon is a closed outline that selects the spots of one tissue
region. Give `addPolygons()` a named vector of polygon files, one for
each section.

``` r
sirup <- addPolygons(sirup, polygons_path = c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv"),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
))

getPolygons(sirup)
#> # A tibble: 19 × 3
#>    polygon_id           sample           vertices        
#>    <chr>                <chr>            <named list>    
#>  1 mg_thymus_slice1::1  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [6 × 6]>
#>  2 mg_thymus_slice1::10 mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [6 × 6]>
#>  3 mg_thymus_slice1::2  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#>  4 mg_thymus_slice1::3  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [5 × 6]>
#>  5 mg_thymus_slice1::4  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [5 × 6]>
#>  6 mg_thymus_slice1::5  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [6 × 6]>
#>  7 mg_thymus_slice1::6  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [8 × 6]>
#>  8 mg_thymus_slice1::7  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [5 × 6]>
#>  9 mg_thymus_slice1::8  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 10 mg_thymus_slice1::9  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [5 × 6]>
#> 11 mg_thymus_slice2::1  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [7 × 6]>
#> 12 mg_thymus_slice2::2  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 13 mg_thymus_slice2::3  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 14 mg_thymus_slice2::4  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 15 mg_thymus_slice2::5  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [6 × 6]>
#> 16 mg_thymus_slice2::6  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [7 × 6]>
#> 17 mg_thymus_slice2::7  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [7 × 6]>
#> 18 mg_thymus_slice2::8  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 19 mg_thymus_slice2::9  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
```

Both files number their eGCs from 1. SIRUP adds the sample to each
polygon ID. `mg_thymus_slice1::1` and `mg_thymus_slice2::1` are
different regions.

``` r
plotSpatialPolygons(sirup, zoom = TRUE, combine_sample_plots = TRUE)
```

``` r
spatialExpressionPlot(
```

## Call clones across all samples

Call clones on the whole receptor table. One clone ID then covers the
sections, the bulk thymus, and the blood.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
dplyr::n_distinct(getReceptors(sirup)$clone_id)
#> [1] 1860
```

## Find where each clone was seen

Each row has a `compartment`. For each clone, the code below counts the
sequences in each compartment. It also records the eGCs that hold the
clone.

``` r
clones <- getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  group_by(clone_id) %>%
  summarise(
    in_section = any(compartment %in% c("thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice2")),
    n_egc = sum(!is.na(polygon_id)),
    egcs = paste(sort(unique(na.omit(polygon_id))), collapse = ", "),
    n_bulk_thymus = sum(compartment == "bulk_thymus"),
    n_blood_month0 = sum(compartment == "blood_month0"),
    n_blood_month12 = sum(compartment == "blood_month12")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    in_egc = n_egc > 0,
    in_blood = n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12 > 0
  )

count(clones, in_egc, in_blood)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   in_egc in_blood     n
#>   <lgl>  <lgl>    <int>
#> 1 FALSE  FALSE     1575
#> 2 FALSE  TRUE       153
#> 3 TRUE   FALSE      121
#> 4 TRUE   TRUE        11
```

The table shows that most clones stay in the thymus. A few eGC clones
also appear in the blood. The SIRUP paper calls these clones exported.
Fisher’s exact test compares the eGC clones with the other clones of the
sections.

``` r
section_clones <- filter(clones, in_section)
fisher.test(table(section_clones$in_egc, section_clones$in_blood))
#> 
#>  Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data
#> 
#> data:  table(section_clones$in_egc, section_clones$in_blood)
#> p-value = 0.3623
#> alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.625789 2.559146
#> sample estimates:
#> odds ratio 
#>   1.326868
```

For each eGC, count the clones that it holds and the clones that reach
the blood.

``` r
getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  filter(!is.na(polygon_id)) %>%
  distinct(polygon_id, clone_id) %>%
  left_join(select(clones, clone_id, in_blood), by = "clone_id") %>%
  group_by(polygon_id) %>%
  summarise(n_clones = n(), n_exported = sum(in_blood)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_exported))
#> # A tibble: 17 × 3
#>    polygon_id           n_clones n_exported
#>    <chr>                   <int>      <int>
#>  1 mg_thymus_slice2::5        23          5
#>  2 mg_thymus_slice2::1        16          3
#>  3 mg_thymus_slice1::10       15          1
#>  4 mg_thymus_slice1::2         2          1
#>  5 mg_thymus_slice2::2        16          1
#>  6 mg_thymus_slice2::3         7          1
#>  7 mg_thymus_slice2::6         4          1
#>  8 mg_thymus_slice1::1         6          0
#>  9 mg_thymus_slice1::3         2          0
#> 10 mg_thymus_slice1::4         1          0
#> 11 mg_thymus_slice1::5        10          0
#> 12 mg_thymus_slice1::6        18          0
#> 13 mg_thymus_slice1::7         2          0
#> 14 mg_thymus_slice1::9         5          0
#> 15 mg_thymus_slice2::7        12          0
#> 16 mg_thymus_slice2::8         4          0
#> 17 mg_thymus_slice2::9         4          0
```

The bundled bulk files hold a subset of the bulk data, and the clones
come from that subset. For the full analysis, see Figure 5 of the SIRUP
paper.

## Measure clonal dominance in each section

Clonal dominance is the share of the receptors in a region that belong
to its largest clones. The regional functions work on all sections at
once. The dominance table has a `sample` column and the full
`polygon_id`. For a longer treatment, see
[Draw tissue regions and measure clonal dominance and diversity](regions.md).

``` r
dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(object = sirup, locus_val = "IGH")

dominance$dominance %>%
  group_by(polygon_id) %>%
  slice_max(proportion, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(sample, polygon_id, clone_id, n_receptors, proportion) %>%
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   sample           polygon_id           clone_id n_receptors proportion
#>   <chr>            <chr>                <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::1  1270               2      0.222
#> 2 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::10 1148               4      0.16 
#> 3 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::2  1661               1      0.5  
#> 4 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::3  1267               2      0.5  
#> 5 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::4  1399               1      1    
#> 6 mg_thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1::5  1385               3      0.231
```

Most plotting functions return a named list with one plot for each
section.

``` r
region_plots <- plotSpatialRegionReceptors(
  dominance = dominance,

  point_size = 1.5,

)
names(region_plots)
```

## Build a tree with blood tips

A lineage tree shows how the sequences of one clone relate to each
other. Each tip of the tree is one sequence. A tree can mix spatial and
bulk sequences. The code below picks an exported eGC clone with blood
sequences from both time points.

``` r
exported <- clones %>%
  filter(in_egc, n_blood_month0 > 0, n_blood_month12 > 0) %>%
  mutate(n_total = n_egc + n_bulk_thymus + n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12) %>%
  filter(n_total <= 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12))
exported
#> # A tibble: 4 × 10
#>   clone_id in_section n_egc egcs    n_bulk_thymus n_blood_month0 n_blood_month12
#>   <chr>    <lgl>      <int> <chr>           <int>          <int>           <int>
#> 1 1045     TRUE           2 mg_thy…            10             15               4
#> 2 1673     TRUE           3 mg_thy…             0              2               1
#> 3 868      TRUE           1 mg_thy…             0              1               2
#> 4 85       TRUE           1 mg_thy…            10              1               1
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: in_egc <lgl>, in_blood <lgl>, n_total <int>

tree_clone <- exported$clone_id[[1]]
tree_section <- sub("::.*$", "", exported$egcs[[1]])
tree_section
#> [1] "mg_thymus_slice2"
```

Make the germline of the clone with `dowser::createGermlines()`. The
germline is the sequence of the unmutated ancestor, and the tree starts
there. Then build the tree. As in
[Call clones and build lineage trees on the tissue](clones-and-trees.md), the germline step
needs the IMGT reference sequences. Set the environment variable
`SIRUP_IMGT_DIR` to the folder that holds them. The tree chunks run only
when that folder exists.

Keep `compartment` in `traits`. The tree plot uses it to set the tip
shapes.

``` r
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id == tree_clone)
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(
  tree_sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  references = dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir),
  id = "sequence_id"
)
#> Warning in fun(sirup_data, ...): 107 sequence lengths longer than predicted
#> germlines, consider setting trim_lengths=TRUE if germlines fail
#> [1] "Read in 1198 from 17 fasta files"
tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  id = "sequence_id",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "sample", "compartment", "polygon_id")
)
set.seed(1)
tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(tree_sirup)
trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees")
```

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` puts the spatial tips on their sections.
Bulk and blood tips appear in the tree only. The argument `shape_by`
sets one shape for each compartment. The argument `color_by` colors the
tips by tree cluster. `clusterTreesTips()` makes the clusters.

``` r
trees <- clusterTreesTips(trees, k = "auto", id = "sequence_id", k_range = 1:6)

pair <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  trees,
  object = sirup,
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  shape_by = "compartment",
  shape_values = c(
    thymus_slice1 = 21, thymus_slice2 = 21, bulk_thymus = 22,
    blood_month0 = 24, blood_month12 = 23
  ),
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = TRUE
)

names(pair)
#> [1] "1045"
```

The list has one element for each clone. If the tips of a clone fall in
more than one section, the list has one element for each clone and
section instead. These elements are named `<clone>::<sample>`. Each one
pairs the full tree with the map of one section. Each element also holds
a `legend` for the tip colors. The function builds it because the call
sets `show_spatial_legend = TRUE`. The code below shows the section that
holds the eGC tips.

``` r
key <- paste0(tree_clone, "::", tree_section)
if (!key %in% names(pair)) key <- tree_clone
section_pair <- pair[[key]]

cowplot::plot_grid(
  cowplot::plot_grid(section_pair$tree, section_pair$spatial_clone, rel_widths = c(1.3, 1)),
  section_pair$legend,
  ncol = 1,
  rel_heights = c(1, section_pair$legend_rel_height)
)
```

![](multisample_files/figure-gfm/tree-plot-show-1.jpeg)

Shapes show the compartment of each tip. Circles are tips from a
section. Squares are bulk thymus. Triangles are blood at the thymectomy.
Diamonds are blood 12 months later. The legend shows the colors, which
are the tree clusters from `clusterTreesTips()`. On the map, a dot has
the color of its tip.
